newsitem.title: USA: U.S. eased law to aid oil firm - report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. eased law to aid oil firm - report.

text.p: The Clinton administration eased a law barring financial transactions between U.S. corporations and countries accused of supporting terrorism to aid a California-based oil firm seeking a stake in a $930 million deal in Sudan, the Washington Post reported on Thursday.

Quoting unidentified federal officials and documents, the newspaper said the August, 1996 exemption to the Antiterrorism Act -- which President Clinton signed just four months earlier -- allowed Occidental Petroleum Corp to seek a share of a major oil deal in Sudan.

The exemption cleared the way for the company to negotiate with the Khartoum government despite the administration's avowed policy of restricting U.S. commerce with Sudan and six other countries blacklisted by the State Department for allegedly supporting terrorism, the Post said.

A State Department official told the newspaper the exemption for Sudan -- and a similar exemption for Syria, also put into effect in August -- did not undercut the Antiterrorism Act because the law permitted the Treasury Department to grant such exemptions.

The exemption for Sudan allowed Occidental to join Canada's Arakis Energy Corp in pursuing the devlopment of a promising but abandoned oil field in southern Sudan containing an estimated 3.5 billion barrels, the Post said.
But the newspaper reported the Sudanese government abruptly excluded Occidental from the Arakis-led consortium in November for "political reasons."
The Syria exemption was intended to encourage participation by Damascus in the Middle East peace process.
